title: [Vantage Point] GCash ends debut flat at P6.60 as early gains fade
summary: Political theater cannot override market valuation

blocks.text: Political theater cannot override market valuation

items: GCash's market debut on October 20, 2023, ended flat at P6.60, despite initial trading interest and the presence of the Philippine president.
Heavy selling pressure and a significant portion of the IPO proceeds coming from secondary shares indicate that market enthusiasm did not translate into sustained demand.
Future performance will depend on Mynt's operating results and investor confidence, with projections suggesting potential price targets between P7.00 and P7.70 in the coming weeks.

Even with the Philippine president gracing its listing bell, GCash finished its much-anticipated market debut right where it started at P6.60. While heavy turnover and an intraday bounce to P6.76 proved that trading interest was real, persistent selling pressure and a secondary-heavy share sale show that political fanfare cannot bypass cold market arithmetic.
Not even the presence of the Philippine president could keep GCash shares above their offer price on their first day of trading.

But writing off the country’s most anticipated market debut after a single session would be premature. One day on the boards cannot determine whether a marquee fintech listing can deliver lasting value.

With President “Bongbong” Ferdinand Marcos Jr. attending the listing bell ceremony on Tuesday, October 20, GCash parent Mynt entered the Philippine Stock Exchange amid lofty expectations that its arrival would energize a sluggish bourse.

In early trading, the stock climbed to an intraday peak of P6.76—roughly 2.42% above its P6.60 offer price. Yet that initial surge quickly met heavy resistance. By the closing bell, the shares had surrendered their modest advance, finishing flat right at P6.60.

It was hardly a quiet debut. Online brokerage DragonFi reported that approximately 1.3 billion shares changed hands. Multiplying that reported volume by the day’s P6.60 to P6.76 trading band yields a calculated turnover between P8.58 billion and P8.79 billion.

That represents massive churn for a stock that ultimately ended exactly where its IPO subscribers started. The offering certainly commanded market attention, but buyers were unwilling to sustain an opening-day premium.

The retreat from P6.76 indicates that sellers became increasingly assertive as the day unfolded. In market parlance, selling pressure overwhelmed buying appetite. Technically, every matched trade requires both a buyer and a seller, but when sellers grow eager enough to accept progressively lower bids, prices naturally slip.

Quick profit-taking explains a good portion of that slide. Retail and institutional subscribers allocated shares at P6.60 had an immediate window to lock in gross gains above that level, even if brokerage commissions and transaction taxes chipped away at their net proceeds.

Conversely, buyers who chased the morning pop near P6.76 ended the day nursing an unrealized loss of roughly 2.37%. Depending on entry price, the very same session felt either like a harmless draw or an immediate disappointment. Everyday familiarity with an app does not alter the arithmetic of trading.

The president’s presence lent the occasion undeniable significance beyond corporate balance sheets. It tethered the listing to Malacañang’s broader push to deepen domestic capital markets and encourage financial inclusion.
For millions of Filipinos who routinely use GCash to send money and settle household bills, owning shares offered a tangible bridge between everyday transactions and corporate ownership.

Yet political theater cannot override market valuation. A ceremonial podium appearance may shine a bright spotlight on the trading floor, but durable demand requires underlying earnings momentum and sustained investor conviction. Retail investors deserve that clear distinction, especially when brand affection makes equity risk seem deceptively simple.
The structure of the offering also demands careful scrutiny. The roughly P60.9-billion transaction delivered only about P10.6 billion in gross primary proceeds to Mynt’s treasury.

A staggering P50.3 billion—approximately 83% of the total—represented secondary shares sold by existing shareholders. Providing liquidity to early venture backers is a standard, legitimate function of an exchange. (READ: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday)

But everyday investors must remember that the vast majority of public capital did not go toward building new servers or expanding product lines; it flowed directly to early owners taking cash off the table.

Can GCASH regain upward momentum in the coming sessions? It is entirely possible. Global funds and domestic institutions that received smaller allocations than requested during bookbuilding could step into the secondary market to build full positions.

Other institutional accounts may simply be waiting for opening-week volatility to subside before deploying capital. Potential demand, however, only matters when buyers actually commit funds at higher price levels.

Vantage Point’s near-term projections remain within reach. Our initial baseline scenario projected the stock settling between P7.00 and P7.70 by October 27, anchored around a P7.40 midpoint. From Tuesday’s P6.60 close, reaching P7.00 requires a 6.1% advance; hitting P7.40 demands 12.1%; and testing P7.70 entails a 16.7% gain. These figures represent analytical benchmarks rather than guaranteed returns.

blocks.text: Tuesday’s flat finish undeniably tempers our early optimism. An intraday high of P6.76 fell short of the lower bound of our weekly target band. Oversubscribed order books and cornerstone commitments failed to spark a runaway opening pop. While our baseline thesis survives its first trial, the market tape offers little justification to elevate our expectations.

The enduring investment case rests squarely on operating performance. In the first half of 2026, Mynt’s net profit grew by just 7.3% to P10.82 billion, while core EBITDA dropped 4% and margins narrowed to 27.3%.

Sharp gains in deposit interest from a P68.6-billion cash balance cushioned the bottom line, but discerning investors must separate operating franchise earnings from passive interest earned on bank balances.

At P6.60, Mynt’s roughly P441.5-billion equity valuation already requires meaningful execution. Our conditional year-end scenario of P7.30 to P8.20 remains grounded on that assumption. The coming days will measure trading conviction; subsequent earnings reports will reveal whether that conviction has real teeth. GCash has captured the market’s undivided attention. It must now earn its premium. – Rappler.com
